comparator.route: Year 2 elective Game Theory (period 5) and year 3 semester 1 Project 3-1 with six elective courses
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme pages (s0, s1, s2) describe the three-year curriculum in words only and give no course list or EC: s1 states that the first year is followed by a second year with mandatory courses plus one elective chosen from two in period 5, and a third year in which students choose three electives per period in periods 1 and 2, and that second-year registration needs 45 first-year credits and third-year registration needs 60 first-year and 40 second-year credits; s2 describes the project-centred, applied approach, the mathematics and programming basis and the courses on knowledge management, cognitive psychology, logic and the philosophy of science. The course-level reconstruction therefore uses the Faculty of Science and Engineering course catalogue for 2025-2026 (s3), the most recent course-level publication reachable from this environment (curriculum.maastrichtuniversity.nl, which holds the current-year courses, was unreachable), and the 2024-2025 catalogue (s4) whose section headings (year 1 core, year 2 core, year 2 electives, year 3 electives, year 3 core) establish which courses are compulsory; the 2025-2026 catalogue lists the same courses in the same order. Period courses carry 4 EC, the semester projects 6 EC and the bachelor's thesis 18 EC. Year 1 totals 60 EC (twelve courses of 4 EC and Projects 1-1 and 1-2), year 2 totals 60 EC (twelve courses of 4 EC, including one period-5 elective, and Projects 2-1 and 2-2) and year 3 totals 60 EC: Project 3-1 (6 EC), six elective courses (24 EC, derived by arithmetic as 30 EC less the project from the catalogue statement that third-year students choose three electives in each of periods 1 and 2 from the optional courses; the space is preserved as two open elective components rather than instantiated), the three core courses of period 4 (Operations Research, Intelligent Systems and Data Analysis, 12 EC) and the 18-EC thesis. In 2025-2026 the year-2 core courses of period 5 are Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence and Linear Programming, and the second-year elective is chosen between Game Theory (KEN2580) and Introduction to Image & Video Processing (KEN3238). The honours tracks (KE@Work, MaRBLe 2.0) and the 30-EC study abroad are alternatives to the project and elective option and are not part of the reconstructed pathway. A human may want to confirm the 2026-2027 course list and the elective structure against the current Education and Examination Regulations.

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic Data Science and Artificial Intelligence bachelor, so no named route applies, but the official curriculum asks second-year students to choose one of two period-5 electives (Game Theory or Introduction to Image & Video Processing) and offers third-year students a semester of project and electives, honours tracks or a semester abroad, and these choices must be instantiated to obtain one 180-EC pathway. The two year-2 electives are equally general and no basis shows that either is more representative of the programme's broad identity, so the first-listed elective in the official curriculum, Game Theory, is used as the neutral tie-break. For year 3 semester 1 the standard route with Project 3-1 and the open elective space is kept, because the honours programme and the semester abroad are explicitly alternatives that replace it rather than the general route.

core: Programming and software: procedural and object-oriented programming, software engineering and databases, learned through project work
Algorithms and computational problem-solving: data structures and algorithms, graph theory and the algorithmic side of data science
Mathematical foundations: discrete mathematics, calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, numerical methods and mathematical modelling
Data science and machine learning: principles of data science, data analysis and machine learning for modelling, analysing and interpreting data
Reasoning, decision-making and intelligent systems: logic, search, planning, optimisation, operations research and intelligent agents
Applied and research practice: semester-long project work on real problems and a bachelor's thesis written as a research paper
adjacent: Cognition, language and human-centred intelligent systems: computational and cognitive neuroscience, human-computer interaction and affective computing, natural language processing, with the programme's courses on cognitive psychology

Philosophy of science and of artificial intelligence: Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence, taught from the philosophy of science and the philosophical issues raised by the pursuit of artificial intelligence

Medical applications of data science and artificial intelligence: medicine named by the programme as a substantive application area, with student projects in healthcare such as software that interprets ultrasound images
Robotics and autonomous systems: robotics presented as an application area for artificial intelligence, and the design of intelligent agents and systems
Logistics and planning: data science and artificial intelligence for planning and decision-making in logistics
questions: How can data and artificial intelligence be used to make better decisions and to solve real-world problems, for example in health?
How can computers learn from data, reason and act intelligently, and how does this relate to human cognition and intelligence?

alternatives.label: Data Science and Artificial Intelligence: Programming, Mathematics, Machine Learning and Reasoning
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has seven courses on mathematics and statistics (Mathematical Methods, Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Advanced Calculus and the applied Research Methods & Statistics), six on computer science (Introduction to Programming, Software Development, Algorithms & Data Structures, Advanced Algorithms, Database Management Systems and Logic & Discrete Mathematics), four on data science and machine learning (Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Image Processing & Computer Vision), four on reasoning and decision-making (Decision-making in AI, Optimization Methods in AI, Reinforcement Learning, AI Ethics), two on statistics and cognition (Statistics & Experimental Methods and Introduction to Brain & Behavior) and Personal & Professional Development. It is therefore a data-science and AI programme grounded in programming and mathematics; the label names these strands and does not present UCR as offering UM's full degree, which also has projects, simulation, natural language processing and a thesis.
alternatives.concept: UM's Data Science and Artificial Intelligence bachelor is organised around programming and software, algorithms, a broad mathematical basis (discrete mathematics, calculus, linear algebra, probability and statistics, numerical methods, mathematical modelling and linear programming), data science and machine learning, reasoning and decision-making for AI (logic, search, planning, optimisation, operations research, intelligent agents), project-centred practice with real problems and a thesis, and a smaller strand on cognition and the philosophy of AI. The strongest defensible UCR response reproduces the core that UCR can teach: programming and software development, algorithms and data structures, databases, a full mathematical track in mathematical methods, linear algebra, probability and statistics, numerical methods, linear systems and advanced calculus, data science, machine learning, deep learning and computer vision, and a decision-and-reasoning strand in logic, search and optimisation, planning under uncertainty and reinforcement learning, with research methods, statistics and a brain-and-behaviour gateway standing in for UM's methods and cognitive-psychology courses. UCR has no graph theory, simulation, natural language processing, human-computer interaction or operations-research course, no semester project and no bachelor thesis, so these stay unmatched.
progression: Introduction to Programming and Logic & Discrete Mathematics open semester 1 and precede every dependent course; Mathematical Methods (semester 2) precedes Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Advanced Calculus and Neural Networks & Deep Learning; Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics and Algorithms & Data Structures (semester 3) precede Software Development, Advanced Algorithms (semester 4) and Machine Learning, Decision-making in AI (semester 5); Machine Learning (semester 5) precedes Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Optimization Methods in AI and Reinforcement Learning (semester 6); the brain-and-behaviour gateway is taken in semester 5 as a stand-alone course with no dependent course.

alternatives.label: Data Science and Artificial Intelligence for Medicine and Health
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has ten courses of data science, machine learning and computing (Introduction to Programming, Introduction to Data Science, Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Image Processing & Computer Vision, Database Management Systems, Algorithms & Data Structures, Decision-making in AI, AI Ethics and Mathematical Methods), five of mathematics and statistics (Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics, Research Methods & Statistics, Statistics & Experimental Methods and Econometrics), seven of biomedicine, public health and health psychology (Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine, Epidemiology & Public Health, Functional Anatomy, Human Physiology, Mechanisms of Disease, Medical & Health Psychology and Introduction to Brain & Behavior), the Advanced Research Seminar on systematic reviews and meta-analysis and Personal & Professional Development. The medical and health setting organises the programme, but more than half of its courses are data-science, computing and statistical methods, so the label names data science and AI applied to medicine and health and does not present it as a medical degree or as UM's full programme.
alternatives.concept: The programme names medicine, together with logistics and robotics, as a substantive area in which data science and artificial intelligence are applied (the programme-interest row on medical applications and the healthcare projects on the programme page). This alternative takes medical applications as its organising logic: it keeps the programming, data-science, statistics and machine-learning methods (including deep learning, image analysis, databases and decision-making under uncertainty) and adds the biomedical and health knowledge in which they are applied, namely foundations of life and health, epidemiology and public health, anatomy, physiology, mechanisms of disease and medical and health psychology, together with research synthesis and causal-inference methods for evaluating health evidence.
progression: Introduction to Programming, Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine and Epidemiology & Public Health open semester 1; Mathematical Methods, Introduction to Data Science and Introduction to Brain & Behavior (semester 2) precede Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics and Machine Learning (semester 3), which precede Neural Networks & Deep Learning (semester 4) and Image Processing & Computer Vision (semester 6); Human Physiology (semester 3), Functional Anatomy (semester 4) and Mechanisms of Disease (semester 6) follow the life-science gateway; Research Methods & Statistics (semester 2) precedes Statistics & Experimental Methods and Medical & Health Psychology (semester 5), which precede the Advanced Research Seminar and Econometrics (semester 6); Algorithms & Data Structures and Decision-making in AI (semester 5) follow Introduction to Programming.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 reproduces UM's technical core (software, algorithms, databases and a broad mathematics track) and treats applications only through its data-science and machine-learning courses; Alternative 2 takes the medical application area named by the programme as its organising logic. It keeps sixteen courses from Alternative 1 (the programming, data-science, machine-learning, statistics, databases, algorithms, decision-making and ethics courses, including Personal & Professional Development) and replaces eight of them (Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Software Development, Advanced Algorithms, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems, Advanced Calculus, Reinforcement Learning and Optimization Methods in AI) with foundations of life and health, epidemiology, anatomy, physiology, mechanisms of disease, medical and health psychology, research synthesis and econometrics. The two programmes differ by 8 courses (60 EC), above the 30 EC / 4-course floor, and the differing courses follow from the change of organising logic: they trade software engineering, applied mathematics and the optimisation and agent-learning courses for the biomedical, public-health and health-evidence knowledge that medical applications need.

alternatives.label: Cognition, Language and Philosophy of Intelligent Systems with Machine Learning
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum has five courses on cognitive science and neuroscience (Introduction to Brain & Behavior, Perception & Action, Higher Order Functions, Psycholinguistics and Statistics & Experimental Methods), four on philosophy and ethics (Introduction to Western Philosophy, Ethics, Philosophy of Mind and AI Ethics), seven on machine learning, AI and robotics (Machine Learning, Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Image Processing & Computer Vision, Decision-making in AI, Optimization Methods in AI, Reinforcement Learning, Robotics), five on programming, data and mathematics (Introduction to Programming, Introduction to Data Science, Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Mathematical Methods, Linear Algebra) and Probability & Statistics, Research Methods & Statistics and Personal & Professional Development. Its organising emphasis is the cognitive, linguistic and philosophical study of intelligence together with machine learning, so the label names cognition, language and philosophy alongside machine learning rather than presenting it as a general data-science degree.
alternatives.concept: The same UM programme also teaches intelligence as a cognitive, linguistic and philosophical subject: Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience, Human Computer Interaction & Affective Computing, Natural Language Processing, Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence, Reasoning Techniques and Intelligent Systems, and its official page names courses on cognitive psychology, logic and the philosophy of science (curricular-topic rows on cognitive psychology and philosophy of science support this direction). This alternative takes that strand as its organising logic: it keeps the programming, mathematics, machine-learning and reasoning spine that AI work needs and replaces software-engineering, database, advanced-algorithm and advanced-mathematics courses with cognitive neuroscience (perception and action, higher-order cognitive functions, psycholinguistics), philosophy of mind, general philosophy, ethics and robotics, so that students study how human and artificial intelligence, language and decision making relate.
progression: Introduction to Programming, Introduction to Data Science and Introduction to Brain & Behavior open semester 1; Mathematical Methods and Perception & Action (semester 2) follow their gateways; Logic & Discrete Mathematics, Linear Algebra, Probability & Statistics and Machine Learning (semester 3) precede Neural Networks & Deep Learning, Optimization Methods in AI and Robotics (semester 4) and Decision-making in AI, Reinforcement Learning and Image Processing & Computer Vision (semesters 5 and 6); Higher Order Functions (semester 5) and Psycholinguistics (semester 6) follow the brain-and-behaviour gateway and Perception & Action; Introduction to Western Philosophy (semester 5) precedes Philosophy of Mind (semester 6), while Ethics (semester 4) has no prerequisite.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 reproduces UM's technical core and Alternative 2 its medical application area; Alternative 3 takes UM's cognitive, linguistic and philosophical strand (Computational and Cognitive Neuroscience, Human Computer Interaction & Affective Computing, Natural Language Processing, Philosophy & Artificial Intelligence) as its organising logic. It keeps seventeen courses from Alternative 1 and fourteen from Alternative 2 (the programming, data-science, mathematics-for-ML, machine-learning, reasoning and decision-making spine, including Personal & Professional Development). Against Alternative 1 it replaces seven courses (Database Management Systems, Software Development, Algorithms & Data Structures, Advanced Algorithms, Computational & Numerical Methods, Linear Systems and Advanced Calculus) with perception and action, higher-order cognitive functions, psycholinguistics, philosophy of mind, introductory philosophy, ethics and robotics; against Alternative 2 it replaces ten courses (the biomedical, public-health and health-evidence courses, databases, algorithms and econometrics) with the same cognitive, philosophical and robotics courses and with logic, optimisation and reinforcement learning. The programme therefore differs from Alternative 1 by 7 courses (52.5 EC) and from Alternative 2 by 10 courses (75 EC), above the 30 EC / 4-course floor in both pairs, and the differing courses follow from the organising logic: they study how human and artificial intelligence, language and decision making relate rather than applying data science in a domain or reproducing the technical core.

selection.assessment: Three UCR alternatives are defensible. Alternative 1 owns the nine generator-eligible rows that describe the programme's technical core (6214 data science and artificial intelligence, 6215 using data to solve real-world problems, 6216 machine learning, 6217 mathematics for artificial intelligence, 6218 programming for data science, 6219 algorithms and computational problem-solving, 6220 modelling and analysing data, 6221 optimisation and better decision-making and 6222 intelligent systems). Alternative 2 follows the medical-applications direction (6224); it shares 16 courses with Alternative 1, so each programme differs from the other by 8 courses (60 EC). Alternative 3 follows the cognition, language and philosophy-of-intelligence strand documented by the official curriculum and programme page and supported by the curricular-topic rows 6226 and 6227; it shares 17 courses with Alternative 1 and 14 with Alternative 2, so it differs from them by 7 and 10 courses (52.5 and 75 EC), and all three pairs pass the 30 EC / 4-course floor. The remaining generator-eligible rows were tested and not included: robotics and autonomous systems (6223) would add only Robotics and Perception & Action to the programming, mathematics, machine-learning and agent courses already in Alternative 1 and both courses are already in Alternative 3, so it was rejected as not-substantively-distinct; artificial intelligence for logistics and planning (6225, with the supporting curricular topic 6229 on simulating complex systems) rests on the planning, optimisation and decision-making courses that Alternative 1 already contains because UCR has no logistics, operations-research or simulation course, so it was rejected as not-substantively-distinct; teaching mathematics (6236, the educational minor described by a programme alumna) rests on education courses that UCR does not offer and was rejected as not-feasible. The curricular-topic row 6228 (knowledge management) generated no alternative because it is support-only and UCR has no knowledge-management course, and the search-only rows (6230 to 6235 and 6237 to 6249) generated no alternative. No row is inherited across split targets.

blocks: Both give a first view of the data-science process of exploring, analysing and modelling data on example data sets; Introduction to Data Science covers data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation and a data research project but has no artificial-intelligence component, whereas UM's course also introduces agents, search and computational intelligence, so the relationship is partial.

Both teach the basics of programming with data types, branching, loops and functions; Introduction to Programming is taught in Python and also covers testing, debugging and object-oriented constructs, while UM's course teaches procedural programming in Java.

Explicitly unmatched: the object-oriented constructs of Objects in Programming (classes, interfaces, polymorphism, event handling and graphical interfaces in Java) are only touched by one part of Introduction to Programming, which is already placed against Procedural Programming.

Both address the software development process: requirements, design, testing and quality assurance, maintenance and code review; Software Development adds programming in C++ and Haskell and does not cover UM's software architectures, design patterns, API development or version control.

Both build a mathematical framework of logic and discrete structures; Logic & Discrete Mathematics applies logic, patterns and structures to computer science and algorithm construction, while UM's course concentrates on logic, proof techniques and the language of mathematics.

Both teach differentiation, integration and differential equations; Mathematical Methods adds complex numbers and applies the techniques in projects, while UM's Calculus also covers limits, sequences and series and multivariable calculus.

Explicitly unmatched: the only UCR logic content sits in Logic & Discrete Mathematics, already placed against Discrete Mathematics, and UCR has no course on propositional and first-order logic systems, semantic tableaux, natural deduction or Hoare logic.
Both introduce linear algebra: systems of linear equations, vectors, matrices, vector spaces and linear transformations.

Both teach numerical methods for continuous mathematics: root finding, numerical differentiation and integration, differential equations and the accuracy of algorithms; UM's course adds floating-point error analysis and interpolation.

Both characterise linear dynamical systems through transfer functions, frequency and impulse response and state-space models; Linear Systems concentrates on linear time-invariant signals and systems, while Mathematical Modelling also treats modelling frameworks, the z-transform and the Laplace transform, stability and pole placement, so the relationship is partial.

Explicitly unmatched: UCR has no course on the simplex algorithm, duality theory and sensitivity analysis; Optimization Methods in AI treats linear and non-linear programming only as laboratory project themes within search and optimisation and is already placed against Reasoning Techniques.

Both teach the design and analysis of algorithms together with data structures and their performance; the UCR course is built around laboratory work and experimental performance analysis, while UM's course treats lists, trees, graphs and strings with their algorithms.

Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course teaches paths, trees, matchings, flows, colourings and connectivity; Advanced Algorithms covers algebraic algorithms and optimisation methods and is not a graph-theory course.

Both teach relational database theory and SQL with data modelling and normalization; Database Management Systems adds authorization and query processing, while UM's course applies the concepts in case studies.

Both cover how data originate and are summarised: research design, experiments and sampling and descriptive and inferential statistics; Research Methods & Statistics does not teach UM's causal reasoning from observational data or data visualisation with Python labs.

Both introduce probability and statistics: probability, distributions, sampling, parameter estimation and the basis of statistical inference; Probability & Statistics also covers simulation, while UM's course adds expectation, moments and limit theorems and hypothesis testing.

Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course teaches discrete-event simulation, Poisson processes, random-number generation and the statistical analysis of simulation output; Probability & Statistics touches simulation only briefly and is already placed against Probability and Statistics.

Both apply statistical models to data: multiple and logistic regression, classification-type models and dimensionality reduction (factor analysis); Statistics & Experimental Methods approaches them as multivariate methods for experimental research, while UM's Data Analysis also covers data inspection and cleaning, tree-based models and the communication of results, so the relationship is partial.

Both teach core machine-learning techniques for classification, regression, clustering and prediction with practical use of the methods; UM's course adds decision trees, Bayesian learning, rule induction and recommender systems.

Both treat language processing with neural methods: Neural Networks & Deep Learning covers text classification and large language models in its second part, which meets UM's language modelling, text classification and the effect of deep learning on NLP; it does not teach statistical NLP, information extraction or dialogue systems, so the relationship is partial.
Reasoning, optimisation, decision-making and intelligent agents

Both teach problem solving by search (blind and informed search, games and adversarial search) and constraint satisfaction; Optimization Methods in AI adds convex and non-linear optimisation and has no logic programming in Prolog, planning in situation calculus or belief networks.

Both address decisions about scarce resources under constraints and uncertainty: Decision-making in AI teaches planning and optimising behaviour in deterministic and non-deterministic, partially observable environments, which meets the stochastic decision problems of Operations Research; it has no network simplex, integer programming or queueing content, so the relationship is partial.

Both treat intelligent agents and the learning of behaviour; Reinforcement Learning builds agents that learn by trial and error with neural networks, while UM's Intelligent Systems covers agent architectures, expert systems, multi-agent cooperation and competition and implements several agent types, so the relationship is partial.

Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course teaches the mathematical theory of strategic games, solution concepts and fairness; Decision-making in AI and Optimization Methods in AI treat adversarial games only as search problems and are already placed elsewhere.
Cognition, interaction, philosophy and ethics of AI

Both introduce the biological and psychological study of cognition: functional brain anatomy, neuronal communication, perception, learning and behaviour; Introduction to Brain & Behavior does not include UM's models of cognition, speech and language or neural networks and genetic algorithms, so the relationship is partial.
Explicitly unmatched: no UCR course teaches the study of user interfaces, interaction design and affective computing.

Both examine philosophical questions raised by artificial intelligence, such as machine intelligence and consciousness, responsibility and the relation between human and artificial cognition; AI Ethics concentrates on ethics, fairness and the moral status of AI systems and adds a psychological perspective, while UM's course starts from the philosophy of science and the quantification of nature.

notes.text: Both programmes include substantial study of programming, mathematics, statistics and machine learning. The Maastricht University Data Science and Artificial Intelligence bachelor additionally includes specialist work in graph theory, simulation, natural language processing, human-computer interaction and operations research, together with semester-long group projects, open electives and a bachelor's thesis. UCR students can instead combine its computer-science, mathematics, data-science, artificial-intelligence and cognitive-science courses, but those specialist components are not offered at the same level of depth.

The Maastricht University Data Science and Artificial Intelligence bachelor organizes study around a fixed sequence of project-centred courses in programming, mathematics, data science and artificial intelligence. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across courses in computer science, mathematics, data science, artificial intelligence and cognitive science. The UCR programmes therefore cover related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the Maastricht programme course by course.
